meta.subtitle: Foodservice distributor compounding per-share earnings through independent-restaurant gains and buybacks

analystSentiment.commentary: We rate US Foods Holding a HOLD with a $98 to $118 target range and a probability-weighted fair value of $104.60; the shares closed at $93.72 on September 28, 2026, and the valuation section sets out the inputs that decide the call. Operations are strong: in Q2'26 (the quarter ended June 27, 2026) net sales rose 4.5% to $10.5 billion, independent-restaurant case volume grew 5.1% and Adjusted EBITDA rose 10.2% to $604 million, and on August 6, 2026 management reaffirmed its FY26 guidance. This republish corrects the debt data. The summary financials now carry a total-debt line, which confirms the same $5.2 billion of net debt the company reports and adds a stricter leverage measure: 3.0x trailing EBITDA, against the company's 2.6x on Adjusted EBITDA. No new debt was found; the correction changes how leverage is measured, not how much there is. The label moves from our earlier BUY to HOLD because of how we now price the scenarios, not because of the debt correction.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: US Foods Holding Corp. markets, sells and distributes fresh, frozen and dry food and non-food products to foodservice customers in the United States, including independent and chain restaurants, healthcare, hospitality, government and education customers. Per its Q2'26 10-Q, it supplies approximately 250,000 customer locations and manages the business as a single operating segment. FY25 revenue was $39.4 billion, up 4.1%, and FY25 net income was $676 million. The company also provides MOXe, an all-in-one foodservice business application. It was incorporated in 2007 and is headquartered in Rosemont, Illinois.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: US Foods is compounding per-share earnings through volume gains with independent restaurants, margin expansion and buybacks, and Q2'26 showed that model working. Against it stand an industry the 10-K describes as low-margin with very low switching costs, the leverage set out in the balance sheet section, and a first half that puts FY26 on track for the low end of its Adjusted EBITDA guidance rather than the midpoint. Our Base holds today's 19.6x forward multiple, so its upside is one year of consensus earnings growth. An earnings stall at a lower multiple would cost more than that, which puts us at HOLD.

catalysts: Independent-restaurant volume: case growth of 5.1% in Q2'26 ran well ahead of total case growth of 1.9%; the growth section carries the argument.
Second-half delivery against reaffirmed FY26 guidance, which includes a 53rd week; the income commentary reads the half-year pace.
Buybacks: $640 million remained under the November 2025 authorization at the end of Q2'26.
Margin: Adjusted EBITDA margin rose 29 basis points year over year in Q2'26.
risks: Consumer demand: the 10-K (February 12, 2026) opens its business risks with spending on food prepared away from home.
Leverage: net debt is 3.0x trailing EBITDA on the stricter measure; the balance sheet section weighs it.
Thin margins: cost moves pass quickly to earnings; the risk section sets out the mechanism.
Competition: the 10-K describes switching costs and barriers to entry as very low.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended Late December.

financials.incomeCommentary:
Q2'26 net sales rose 4.5% to $10.5 billion, which the company attributes to case-volume growth and food-cost inflation of 2.3%; total case volume rose 1.9%. Gross profit rose 8.0% to $1.9 billion, or 18.2% of sales, which the company credits to higher volume, improved cost of goods sold and a $19 million favorable year-over-year LIFO adjustment. Operating expenses grew 5.1%, slower than gross profit, and operating income reached $443 million, a 4.2% margin. Net income rose 22.8% to $275 million and GAAP diluted EPS rose 29.2% to $1.24. On the company's adjusted measures, Adjusted EBITDA rose 10.2% to $604 million at a 5.7% margin and Adjusted Diluted EPS rose 21.0% to $1.44.

For the 26 weeks ended June 27, 2026, Adjusted EBITDA rose from $937 million to $1,017 million, a pace just below the low end of the full-year guidance set out next, and gross profit absorbed $33 million of LIFO expense. The FY26 guidance, given on February 12, 2026 and reaffirmed on August 6, calls for 4% to 6% net-sales growth, 9% to 13% Adjusted EBITDA growth and 18% to 24% Adjusted Diluted EPS growth, including a 53rd week the company expects to add approximately 1% to Adjusted EBITDA growth. Both half-year periods have the same number of weeks, so that extra week falls in the second half, and it is about the size of the half-year shortfall. The half-year pace therefore puts FY26 on track for the low end of guidance, not the midpoint.

On the annual series, FY25 revenue was $39.4 billion, up 4.1%, at a gross margin of 17.4% and an operating margin of 3.0%, and FY25 GAAP diluted EPS was $2.94. The 2026 proxy (April 2, 2026) gives FY25 Adjusted Diluted EPS of $3.98, the base from which the company's EPS guidance grows. We use the GAAP series for history and the adjusted figure only to read the guidance. Consensus EPS of $4.78 for FY26E and $5.55 for FY27E sits far above the GAAP history; the consensus data do not state their basis, and we use them as given.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended Late December.

financials.balanceCommentary:
Total debt rose from $4.7 billion at FY23 to $4.9 billion at FY24 and $5.2 billion at FY25, and net debt rose from $4.4 billion to the same level as total debt. The August 6 release reports Net Debt at that same level at the end of Q2'26 and a ratio of Net Debt to Adjusted EBITDA of 2.6x, down from 2.7x at the end of FY25. The two net-debt figures agree. The ratios differ in the denominator. The company divides by Adjusted EBITDA, which adds back share-based compensation, LIFO reserve adjustments, restructuring charges and business transformation costs, while the page's 3.0x trailing ratio uses EBITDA before those adjustments. FY25 shows the size of the gap, with EBITDA of $1.7 billion in the summary table and Adjusted EBITDA of $1.932 billion in the proxy. We use the page's ratio as the stricter measure.

Leverage at that level is what a low-margin earner carries into a downturn: if EBITDA falls, the ratio rises with no change in debt, and equity holders bear the difference. The ratio held steady over FY23 to FY25 because EBITDA grew, from $1.4 billion in FY23 to the FY25 level above, not because debt fell. Trailing interest coverage of 4.1x, with net interest expense of $77 million in Q2'26, is serviceable while EBITDA grows.

Liquidity is a separate and smaller point. Cash and short-term investments fell from $0.3 billion at FY23 to $0.0 billion in the rounded table, and the current ratio fell to 1.16 at FY25 and 1.14 on a trailing basis. The company runs with little cash on hand, which limits flexibility but does not add to the net debt that sets equity risk. Total equity declined to $4.3 billion at FY25 from a higher FY23 level as repurchases returned capital.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended Late December.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation is steady. FY25 free cash flow was $959 million after capital expenditure of $410 million, a 2.4% FCF margin, and the trailing FCF yield is 4.7%. Year to date through June 27, 2026, operating cash flow was $725 million, the same as a year earlier; the company explains that higher net income was offset by favorable changes in operating assets and liabilities in the prior-year period. First-half capital expenditure of $174 million went to information technology, property and equipment and distribution facilities, and free cash flow was $552 million against $569 million a year earlier. The company pays no dividend; the capital allocation section weighs where free cash flow goes.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: At $93.72 the shares trade at 28.8x trailing earnings, 0.5x sales and 14.7x trailing EV/EBITDA, the last of which counts the $5.2 billion of net debt. On consensus estimates the P/E falls to 19.6x next-twelve-months and ~16.9x FY27E; the income commentary notes that the estimates' basis is not stated. Because we value the shares a year out on FY27E EPS, when FY27 will be the forward year, the like-for-like reference for every scenario multiple is today's next-twelve-months multiple, not the FY27E one. No peer multiples are available, so we value the shares on their own forward earnings, anchoring each scenario to a consensus EPS figure and a stated multiple. The shares sit between the $69.88 low and the $111.42 high of their 52-week range. The page's price history shows a sharp fall in September: the shares traded near the top of that range in late August and dropped to around today's level by mid-September, with the steepest one-day fall in the second week of the month. No source we have explains the decline, and we do not supply a reason. We assume neither that it reverses nor that it deepens: the Base holds today's forward multiple, and the Bull is the case in which the fall reverses.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Independent-restaurant volume growth holds near Q2'26's pace, FY26 reaches the top of the 18% to 24% Adjusted Diluted EPS guidance, and the forward multiple recovers from today's 19.6x to the higher level the shares carried in late August, before the September fall, applied to FY27E consensus EPS of $5.55. Implied $125, between the $120.00 median and the $130.00 top analyst target.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Volume and margin gains continue at a slower pace and FY27 EPS meets consensus. A year out we hold today's forward multiple and apply it to FY27E EPS, so the upside is one year of consensus earnings growth at an unchanged multiple, not a re-rating. Slowing consensus growth after FY26, the leverage in the balance sheet section and low margins argue against a higher multiple; Q2'26 results and reaffirmed guidance argue against a lower one. Implied $109, below the $116.67 consensus target.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: A consumer pullback flattens volumes and cost deflation or a pass-through lag squeezes margins. With half of FY26 reported and guidance reaffirmed, the hit lands on FY27, whose EPS stalls at the FY26E $4.78 instead of growing. We apply 14x, between a quarter and a third below today's forward multiple; the scenario commentary argues the figure. Implied $67, below the $69.88 52-week low and above the $65.00 lowest analyst target.

valuation.scenarioCommentary:
Weighting Bull at 25%, Base at 55% and Bear at 20% gives weighted values of $31.25, $59.95 and $13.40 and a fair value of $104.60. Expected upside is 11.6%, bear-case downside is 28.5% and reward/risk is 0.41x. Expected upside clears the +10.0% BUY threshold but reward/risk falls short of 0.50x, so the derived label is HOLD.

The call sits on the line, and the deciding input is the Bear multiple. At about 15x on the same stalled EPS, or with a Base multiple about one turn above today's forward multiple, the label derives BUY. For the higher Bear multiple: the trailing FCF yield of 4.7% funds buybacks, and interest coverage of 4.1x leaves the debt serviceable, both of which support the valuation in a downturn. For the lower one: the leverage mechanism set out in the balance sheet section means the equity's multiple compresses more than the business's when EBITDA falls, a 3.0% operating margin leaves little to absorb a pullback, and management's stated aim of holding net leverage at 2.6x would leave less room for buybacks as EBITDA fell, which weakens the buyback argument. The shares have also traded below the higher alternative's implied price within the past year, at their 52-week low. On balance the leverage points weigh more with us, and we use 14x; that is a judgment, not a finding.

The label also depends on the price. On these fixed scenarios, only the lowest mid-September close in the page's history derives BUY, every other close in it derives HOLD, and closes near the 52-week high would derive SELL.

The weights reflect our view of each story. The Base carries the most weight because Q2'26 volumes accelerated and guidance was reaffirmed. The Bull carries less because it needs both a top-of-guidance year and a full recovery of the September fall. The Bear carries the least because a pullback within a year is possible, but on August 6 the CEO described a "challenging but stable industry environment", so we do not make it the central case.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: US Foods manages its business as a single operating segment, a broadline distributor serving approximately 250,000 customer locations through more than 70 distribution facilities, a fleet of over 6,500 trucks and over 90 cash and carry locations, per the Q2'26 10-Q. In Q2'26 total case volume grew 1.9%: independent-restaurant volume rose 5.1%, healthcare 3.5% and hospitality 4.4%, partially offset by a 1.5% decrease in chain volume. The offer to customers rests on Exclusive Brands, the MOX business platform and the Pronto delivery program, supported by over 4,000 sales associates.

moatFactors.name: National scale and network
moatFactors.body: The network lets the company, in its words, leverage its "nationwide scale and footprint while executing locally." The 10-K tempers that: certain competitors may have greater scale in certain markets, and regional and local distributors may have a lower cost to serve due to geographic proximity. Scale is an advantage against small rivals, not a barrier to them.

moatFactors.name: Exclusive Brands and MOX
moatFactors.body: The company says its customer relationships are further strengthened by the MOX digital platform, which helps customers manage orders and inventories, and it leads its customer promise with the Exclusive Brands portfolio. Gross margin rose from 16.1% in FY22 to 17.4% in FY25 and 17.6% on a trailing basis, consistent with a better mix, though no source ties the gain to these programs.

moatFactors.name: Low switching costs
moatFactors.body: The 10-K states that "the cost of switching distributors is very low, as are the barriers to entry," that the company generally does not have exclusive distribution agreements with customers, and that it competes with national, regional and local distributors, cash-and-carry operations, warehouse clubs and online wholesalers. That caps pricing power and is the main reason the moat is narrow.

businessMoat.durability: The moat is narrow. Scale, a national network and the company's own brands and tools give US Foods a cost and service edge, and Q2'26 shows it adding volume in the channels it targets. By the 10-K's own account, though, customers can switch cheaply and entry barriers are very low, so the edge has to be re-earned through service and price rather than held through lock-in. Durability is therefore an execution question rather than a structural one.

points: Independent restaurants: organic independent case volume rose 5.0% in Q2'26 and 4.7% over the 26 weeks, against total organic volume growth of 1.7% and 1.4%. Sustaining that gap is the core of the growth case.

Plan delivery: the CEO said Q2'26 results, including 10% Adjusted EBITDA growth and 21% Adjusted Diluted EPS growth, were "in line with our long-range plan." The proxy called 2025 a strong start to that three-year plan, and the record so far supports the claim.
Top line: consensus revenue of ~$41.5B for FY26E (+5%) and $43.2B for FY27E assumes mid-single-digit growth continues, consistent with the 4% to 6% FY26 guidance, which includes a 53rd week.
Per-share growth: consensus EPS rises from $4.78 for FY26E to $5.55 for FY27E, faster than revenue, which requires continued margin gains and a shrinking share count.

management.leadership: Per the 2026 proxy, filed April 2, 2026, the fiscal 2025 named executive officers were David E. Flitman, Chief Executive Officer; Dirk J. Locascio, Executive Vice President, Chief Financial Officer; Steven M. Guberman, Executive Vice President, Chief Transformation Officer and Nationally Managed Business; Randy J. Taylor, Executive Vice President, Field Operations and Local Sales; and John A. Tonnison, Executive Vice President, Chief Information and Digital Officer. The August 6, 2026 release identifies Mr. Flitman as Chair of the Board and CEO. Management frames its results against a three-year long-range plan, and the growth section weighs how far the record supports that framing.
management.capitalAllocation: US Foods pays no dividend and returns cash through buybacks. It repurchased $926 million of stock in FY25 and, over the 26 weeks ended June 27, 2026, 5.8 million shares for approximately $500 million, including 4.4 million shares for $374 million in Q2'26; $640 million remained under the November 2025 authorization. The cover-page share count of 216.33M is below the count at the March 18, 2026 proxy record date. Across FY24 and FY25, repurchases ran at about the level of free cash flow while total debt rose, so no free cash flow went to debt reduction; the summary table does not show what the added debt funded. On August 6 the CFO said the company is "maintaining our net leverage at 2.6 times", which on the Adjusted EBITDA basis means debt grows with EBITDA. We think that is a reasonable choice while earnings grow and the shares trade below our fair value, but it leaves deleveraging as a step management would have to take later if earnings stalled.
management.governance: The captured proxy excerpt covers pay, ownership and the related-party policy, not board composition, so we do not assess board independence. The Chair and CEO roles are combined in Mr. Flitman, per the August 6 release. Per the 2026 proxy, Say-on-Pay received 96% approval in the prior year's vote, the Compensation and Human Capital Committee kept the FY25 incentive design similar to FY24, and Mr. Flitman's base salary rose 7.7% to $1,400,000 effective January 1, 2025. The FY25 annual incentive plan weighted Adjusted EBITDA at 70%, distribution cost per case at 15% and "IND Market Share" at 15%. Because Adjusted EBITDA excludes share-based compensation and LIFO effects, the main pay metric rewards a measure that sits above GAAP earnings. The Audit Committee reviews related-party transactions under a written policy. For outside holders the record is orderly rather than distinctive.
management.insiderOwnership: As of the March 18, 2026 record date, per the 2026 proxy, directors and executive officers as a group (17 people) held 1,627,541 shares, less than 1% of the 220,242,295 outstanding, and Mr. Flitman held 319,221 shares. Six institutions reported stakes above 5%: The Vanguard Group (11.0%), Blackrock (8.8%), Boston Partners (7.0%), FMR LLC (6.9%), Wellington Management Group LLP (5.8%) and Capital World Investors (5.3%). The Vanguard figure rests on a Schedule 13G amendment as of November 29, 2024 and the Blackrock figure on a Schedule 13G as of December 31, 2023, so both may be out of date; the excerpt does not carry the dates behind the other four. No holder approaches control, so outside holders face no dominant shareholder, and alignment rests on pay design rather than on insider stakes, which are small.

idiosyncratic: Demand: the 10-K opens its business risks with consumer spending on food prepared away from home, which an economic downturn may reduce. Chain volume already fell in Q2'26, offset by gains in other channels. A broad volume decline is the Bear's trigger.

Margin sensitivity: the 10-K says profit levels may be negatively affected during product cost deflation even when the gross profit percentage stays constant, and rapid inflation may reduce margins if there is a lag in passing costs on. With FY25 operating margin of 3.0%, small cost moves reach earnings quickly.

Debt terms: the release's forward-looking statements list the level of interest rates, the availability of indebtedness and restrictions under the agreements governing it among the factors that could affect results, so refinancing terms matter as well as the amount of debt.
Structural demand: the release's forward-looking statements name advancements in pharmaceutical therapies as a factor that may reduce the consumption of food prepared away from home.
risks.systemic: The 10-K describes U.S. foodservice distribution as sensitive to national, regional and local economic conditions, and cites tariffs, trade policies, inflationary pressure and supply chain disruptions among the factors that could weigh on consumer confidence and discretionary spending. Interest rates matter through the cost and availability of debt and through the multiple the market pays for a leveraged distributor.

body: We rate US Foods Holding a HOLD with a $98 to $118 target range around a fair value of $104.60. The business is executing and management reaffirmed FY26 guidance, but holding today's forward multiple yields one year of consensus earnings growth, and an earnings stall at a lower multiple would cost more. The valuation section sets out the Bear multiple and the price levels that decide the call.

We would move to BUY on evidence that raises the Bull weight or the Base: second-half results that put FY26 Adjusted EBITDA growth toward the midpoint of guidance while independent-restaurant volume growth holds near its Q2'26 pace. We would lower our fair value if FY26 Adjusted EBITDA growth falls below the 9% low end of guidance even with the 53rd week included, or if total case volume turns negative.
